reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder of sex development in 46,XY individuals caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene
Complete androgen insensitivity produces a typical female external phenotype with a blind-ending vagina and absent uterus
May present as primary amenorrhoea, absent pubic and axillary hair, or an inguinal hernia containing a testis
Testes are present and produce anti-Mullerian hormone, so Mullerian structures regress and the uterus is absent
Testosterone levels are typically in or above the normal male range but cannot act because of receptor resistance
Partial androgen insensitivity produces a spectrum of undervirilised or ambiguous genitalia depending on residual receptor function
There is a risk of gonadal tumours in retained intra-abdominal testes, informing decisions about gonadal management
reference.pathophysiology: The androgen receptor mediates the actions of testosterone and dihydrotestosterone that drive male genital and somatic development. In androgen insensitivity syndrome, mutations in the X-linked androgen receptor gene impair or abolish receptor function, so target tissues cannot respond to circulating androgens despite normal or elevated testosterone. In 46,XY individuals the testes still secrete anti-Mullerian hormone, causing regression of Mullerian structures, but the failure of androgen action prevents virilisation of the external genitalia and Wolffian development. The degree of residual receptor activity determines whether the phenotype is complete, partial or minimal.
additionalInvestigations: Testosterone, luteinising hormone and anti-Mullerian hormone measurement
Pelvic imaging to demonstrate absent uterus and locate the gonads
Molecular genetic testing of the androgen receptor gene
Assessment of the ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone to help distinguish 5-alpha-reductase deficiency
redFlags: An inguinal or labial mass in a phenotypically female child that may be a testis
Primary amenorrhoea with absent sexual hair prompting evaluation for a disorder of sex development
Ambiguous genitalia in a newborn requiring urgent specialist assessment
Concern about malignant change in retained intra-abdominal gonads
reference.prognosis: With appropriate multidisciplinary care, including psychological support, sex steroid management and individualised decisions about gonadal retention or removal, outcomes are generally good, though fertility is not possible and gender identity should guide management.
pitfalls: Assuming a phenotypically female patient with primary amenorrhoea has a uterus and ovaries
Misdiagnosing partial androgen insensitivity as a biosynthetic defect without receptor testing
Neglecting the gonadal tumour risk when planning long-term gonadal management
Overlooking the psychological and identity dimensions of disorders of sex development care
